details:
**Jibril (Gabriel) and "Recite!"**
The archangel who revealed the Quran to Muhammad. On the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), he appeared to Muhammad in the cave on Mount Hira and commanded him to "Recite!" (or "Read!"), beginning the revelation. In Islam he also brought the winged steed Buraq for Muhammad's Night Journey (Isra) and announced Jesus's birth to Maryam.

**Munkar and Nakir**
Two angels who question the dead in their graves about their faith (who their Lord, prophet, and religion are). This "examination" takes place in barzakh, the intermediate state between death and the Day of Judgment.

**Raqib and Atid (Kiraman Katibin)**
The "Honorable Scribes," two angels who sit on each person's shoulders: one records good deeds and the other records bad deeds. Their record is presented on Judgment Day.

**Michael and Gabriel (archangels)**
The best-known archangels in Judaism and Christianity. Michael is the warrior leader of God's armies, and Gabriel is God's messenger. They are the most common giveaway names for angels.

**The Annunciation**
The Gospel of Luke's account in which the angel Gabriel tells the Virgin Mary she will bear Jesus, saying "Fear not, Mary: for thou hast found favour with God."

**Seraphim, cherubim, and ophanim**
Classes of angels in the Hebrew Bible and Jewish tradition. Seraphim are six-winged beings around God's throne in Isaiah; cherubim guard Eden and flank the Ark of the Covenant; and the ophanim ("wheels") are described as wheels covered with eyes, from Ezekiel's vision of God's chariot.

**Pseudo-Dionysius's celestial hierarchy**
The late-antique Christian writer Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite arranged angels into nine choirs in three tiers: Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones; Dominions, Virtues, and Powers; and Principalities, Archangels, and Angels.

**Azrael (Azrail), the angel of death**
The Islamic angel who takes the souls of the dead, often compared to the Grim Reaper. In a hadith, when the angel of death came for Moses, Moses slapped him; God then offered Moses as many extra years as the hairs his hand covered on an ox's back, but Moses chose to die.

**Harut and Marut**
Two angels mentioned in the Quran who taught sorcery to the people of Babylon while warning that it was a trial. Later legend says they were sent to Earth, were tempted by a beautiful woman named Zuhra (associated with the planet Venus), and fell into sin.

**Maalik and the guardians of Jahannam**
Maalik is the angel who rules over Jahannam (hell) in Islam. The Quran says nineteen angels, known as the Zabaniyah, guard hell under him.

**Belief in angels as an article of faith**
Belief in angels (malaika) is the second of the six articles of Islamic faith, after belief in God. In Islam, angels are made of light, unlike the jinn, who are made of smokeless fire.

**Iblis refusing to bow to Adam**
In the Quran, God ordered the angels to bow to Adam, but Iblis refused out of pride and became Shaytan (Satan). Iblis is described as a jinn, so whether he was ever truly an angel is debated. In the same story, Adam proves his superiority by knowing the names of things that the angels did not know.

**Lot's visitors and Sodom**
In Genesis, two angels visit Lot in Sodom before God destroys the city. When a mob demands that he hand over his guests, Lot offers his own daughters instead; the angels then strike the mob blind and lead Lot's family out.

**Balaam's donkey**
In the Book of Numbers, an angel with a drawn sword blocks the path of the prophet Balaam. His donkey sees the angel and refuses to go on, and is miraculously given speech to rebuke Balaam for beating her.

**The empty tomb of Jesus**
According to the Gospel of Matthew, an angel descended, rolled away the stone from Jesus's tomb, sat on it, and told the women who came that Jesus had risen.
